title: Comparing: comparatives and superlatives
objectives: I can form the comparative of an adjective with '-іш-' or '-ш-', including the stem changes in 'ви́щий', 'ни́жчий' and 'доро́жчий', and use the four comparatives on other stems: 'кра́щий', 'гі́рший', 'бі́льший' and 'ме́нший'.
I can compare people, places and seasons, naming what something is compared with by 'ніж' or by 'за' with the accusative, and say how big the difference is and who in a family is older or younger.
I can form the superlative with 'най-', say 'as ... as possible' with 'якнай-', and use 'більш' and 'менш' with an adjective.
I can compare actions with comparative adverbs such as 'кра́ще' and 'шви́дше', and say that two things are equal or not equal with 'таки́й ..., як', 'таки́й са́мий, як' and 'так са́мо, як'.
I can explain why 'ле́гший' has the sound [x], and why 'висо́кий' and 'низьки́й' become 'ви́щий' and 'ни́жчий'.

vocabulary.note: The comparative of 'до́брий', good, and of 'га́рний' when it means good. It is formed on a different stem from both, as English 'better' is from 'good'. It declines like 'нови́й': 'кра́ща', 'кра́ще', 'кра́щі'.

example.source: The coffee is better today than yesterday.

vocabulary.note: Its comparative is 'гі́рший', worse, on another stem. The adverb is 'пога́но', badly, from the unit on the present tense.
The comparative of 'пога́ний'. It declines like 'нови́й': 'гі́рша', 'гі́рше', 'гі́рші'. The superlative 'найгі́рший' means worst.

example.source: This film is worse than the book.

vocabulary.note: The superlative of 'до́брий' and 'га́рний': the prefix 'най-' before the comparative 'кра́щий', with the stress where 'кра́щий' has it. Ukrainian has no word for 'the', so 'найкра́щий' alone means 'the best'.

example.source: This is the best coffee in Kyiv.

vocabulary.note: It describes people, buildings and mountains. The comparative is 'ви́щий', taller or higher: the '-ок-' of the stem drops, and 'с' with the suffix '-ш-' is written 'щ'.
The comparative is 'ни́жчий': the '-ьк-' of the stem drops, and 'з' with the suffix '-ш-' is written 'жч'. Of a person, 'невисо́кий', not tall, is more usual and kinder.
It describes length and time: 'до́вга ву́лиця', 'до́вгий день'. The comparative is 'до́вший', with the 'г' dropped. The adverb 'до́вго', for a long time, is from the unit on the past.

example.source: In June the days are long.

vocabulary.note: It describes length and time, never a person's height. The comparative is 'коро́тший', with the '-к-' dropped.
The comparative is 'моло́дший', younger, with the stress moved to the stem. With family words it says who was born later: 'моло́дший брат', younger brother.
It means light for weight and easy for a task. The comparative is 'ле́гший', with the '-к-' dropped and the stress on the stem. In both words the 'г' is said [x]. The adverb is 'ле́гко', easily.
It means heavy for weight and difficult for a task. The comparative is 'ва́жчий': the '-к-' drops, and 'ж' with the suffix '-ш-' is written 'жч'.

example.source: We have a hard day today.

vocabulary.note: The comparative is 'теплі́ший'. The adjective describes a thing ('те́плий день', 'те́пла ку́ртка'); the predicative word 'те́пло' says that it is warm ('Сього́дні те́пло.').

example.source: In winter you need to wear a warm jacket.

vocabulary.note: The comparative is 'холодні́ший', with the stress on the suffix. The predicative word 'хо́лодно', it is cold, has the stress on the first syllable.
The comparative is 'шви́дший', with the '-к-' dropped. The adverb is 'шви́дко', quickly, and its comparative 'шви́дше', faster.

example.source: The train to Lviv is very fast.

vocabulary.note: It introduces the second thing in a comparison, in the same case as the first, and a comma stands before it. A different word with the same spelling is the masculine noun 'ніж', knife, genitive 'ножа́'.

example.source: My brother is older than I am.

vocabulary.note: The comparative of 'бага́то', a lot. It goes with a verb ('Я бі́льше чита́ю.') or, like 'бага́то', with a noun in the genitive ('бі́льше ча́су', more time). The superlative is 'найбі́льше', most.
The comparative of 'ма́ло', little. It goes with a verb or with a noun in the genitive ('ме́нше люде́й', fewer people). The superlative is 'найме́нше', least.
It agrees like an adjective: 'така́', 'таке́', 'такі́'. Before an adjective it means 'so' ('таки́й вели́кий'), and with 'як' it compares: 'не таки́й вели́кий, як', not as big as.

example.target: Львів не таки́й вели́кий, як Ки́їв.
example.source: Lviv is not as big as Kyiv.
example.source_literal: Lviv not such big, as Kyiv.

dialogues.title: Kyiv or Lviv?
dialogues.context: Sam has just come back from a weekend in Lviv and meets Oksana at Andrii's café. The two friends say 'ти' to each other. 'Як тобі́ Львів?', literally 'how to-you Lviv?', means 'How do you like Lviv?'.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Се́ме, приві́т! Як тобі́ Львів?
lines.source: Hi, Sam! How did you like Lviv?
lines.source_literal: Sam, hi! How to-you Lviv?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Мені́ ду́же сподо́бався! Він ме́нший, ніж Ки́їв, але́ ду́же га́рний.
lines.source: I really liked it! It's smaller than Kyiv, but very beautiful.
lines.source_literal: To-me very pleased! It smaller, than Kyiv, but very beautiful.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: А стари́й центр? Він кра́щий, ніж у Ки́єві?
lines.source: And the old center? Is it better than in Kyiv?
lines.source_literal: And old center? It better, than in Kyiv?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Мо́жливо. Там ду́же ціка́ві музе́ї й найкра́ща ка́ва в Украї́ні!
lines.source: Maybe. The museums there are very interesting, and the coffee is the best in Ukraine!
lines.source_literal: Possibly. There very interesting museums and best coffee in Ukraine!

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Найкра́ща ка́ва? Андрі́й тебе́ чу́є!
lines.source: The best coffee? Andrii can hear you!
lines.source_literal: Best coffee? Andrii you hears!

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ка́ва в Андрі́я, звича́йно, ще кра́ща!
lines.source: Andrii's coffee is even better, of course!
lines.source_literal: Coffee at Andrii, of-course, even better!

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: А яке́ мі́сто тобі́ бі́льше подо́бається?
lines.source: And which city do you like more?
lines.source_literal: And which city to-you more pleases?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ки́їв. Він бі́льший і ціка́віший, і тут мої́ дру́зі.
lines.source: Kyiv. It's bigger and more interesting, and my friends are here.
lines.source_literal: Kyiv. It bigger and more-interesting, and here my friends.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: А пого́да? У Льво́ві теплі́ше чи холодні́ше, ніж тут?
lines.source: And the weather? Is it warmer or colder in Lviv than here?
lines.source_literal: And weather? In Lviv warmer or colder, than here?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Тро́хи холодні́ше. І там ча́сто йде дощ.
lines.source: A little colder. And it often rains there.
lines.source_literal: A-little colder. And there often goes rain.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Так, у Льво́ві бі́льше дощі́в, ніж у Ки́єві.
lines.source: Yes, Lviv gets more rain than Kyiv.
lines.source_literal: Yes, in Lviv more of-rains, than in Kyiv.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Насту́пного лі́та ми пої́демо туди́ ра́зом, до́бре?
lines.source: Next summer we'll go there together, OK?
lines.source_literal: Of-next of-summer we will-go there together, good?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: До́бре! Але́ я візьму́ найтеплі́шу ку́ртку!
lines.source: OK! But I'll take my warmest jacket!
lines.source_literal: Good! But I will-take warmest jacket!

dialogues.title: Winter or summer?
dialogues.context: On a snowy evening in January, Taras visits his sister Olena, who is three years older than he is. Brother and sister say 'ти' to each other. 'На ву́лиці', literally 'on street', also means outdoors.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Оле́но, на ву́лиці так хо́лодно! Сього́дні холодні́ше, ніж учо́ра.
lines.source: Olena, it's so cold outside! It's colder today than yesterday.
lines.source_literal: Olena, on street so cold! Today colder, than yesterday.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: А мені́ подо́бається зима́. Вона́ кра́ща, ніж лі́то.
lines.source: But I like winter. It's better than summer.
lines.source_literal: And to-me pleases winter. It better, than summer.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Чому́? Улі́тку теплі́ше й дні до́вші.
lines.source: Why? In summer it's warmer and the days are longer.
lines.source_literal: Why? In-summer warmer and days longer.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Але́ взи́мку мі́сто таке́ бі́ле й га́рне!
lines.source: But in winter the city is so white and beautiful!
lines.source_literal: But in-winter city such white and beautiful!

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: А я бі́льше люблю́ лі́то. Улі́тку мо́жна ї́здити на мо́ре.
lines.source: And I like summer more. In summer you can go to the sea.
lines.source_literal: And I more love summer. In-summer possible to-go on sea.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Ти завжди́ так ка́жеш. Але́ я ста́рша, і я зна́ю кра́ще!
lines.source: You always say that. But I'm older, and I know better!
lines.source_literal: You always so say. But I older, and I know better!

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Так, ти ста́рша на три ро́ки. Але́ я ви́щий за те́бе!
lines.source: Yes, you're three years older. But I'm taller than you!
lines.source_literal: Yes, you older on three years. But I taller than you!

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Ви́щий, так. А хто з нас кра́ще ва́рить борщ?
lines.source: Taller, yes. But which of us cooks borscht better?
lines.source_literal: Taller, yes. And who from us better cooks borscht?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ма́ма, звича́йно. Її́ борщ найкра́щий.
lines.source: Mom, of course. Her borscht is the best.
lines.source_literal: Mom, of-course. Her borscht best.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Так. А взи́мку борщ ще смачні́ший!
lines.source: True. And in winter borscht is even tastier!
lines.source_literal: Yes. And in-winter borscht even tastier!

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: До́бре, зима́ не така́ пога́на, як я ду́мав.
lines.source: All right, winter isn't as bad as I thought.
lines.source_literal: Good, winter not such bad, as I thought.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Ось ба́чиш! Ста́рша сестра́ завжди́ зна́є кра́ще.
lines.source: There, you see! An older sister always knows best.
lines.source_literal: Here you-see! Older sister always knows better.

dialogues.title: Which language is harder?
dialogues.context: After class, Sam stays to talk with his teacher Iryna Petrivna. Teacher and student say 'ви' to each other.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Іри́но Петрі́вно, яка́ мо́ва ва́жча, украї́нська чи англі́йська?
lines.source: Iryna Petrivna, which language is harder, Ukrainian or English?
lines.source_literal: Iryna Petrivna, which language more-difficult, Ukrainian or English?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Для вас, напе́вно, украї́нська. А для ме́не ва́жча англі́йська.
lines.source: For you, probably Ukrainian. And for me, English is harder.
lines.source_literal: For you, probably, Ukrainian. And for me more-difficult English.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Чому́? Украї́нська грама́тика наба́гато ва́жча за англі́йську.
lines.source: Why? Ukrainian grammar is much harder than English grammar.
lines.source_literal: Why? Ukrainian grammar much more-difficult than English.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Так, вона́ ва́жча. Але́ ми пи́шемо так, як гово́римо.
lines.source: Yes, it is harder. But we write the way we speak.
lines.source_literal: Yes, it more-difficult. But we write so, as we-speak.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, чита́ти украї́нською ле́гше, ніж я ду́мав.
lines.source: Yes, reading in Ukrainian is easier than I thought.
lines.source_literal: Yes, to-read in-Ukrainian easier, than I thought.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: А говори́ти? Ви вже гово́рите наба́гато кра́ще, ніж пе́ршого ти́жня.
lines.source: And speaking? You already speak much better than in the first week.
lines.source_literal: And to-speak? You already speak much better, than of-first of-week.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Дя́кую! Але́ я ще говорю́ пові́льніше, ніж Окса́на й Тара́с.
lines.source: Thank you! But I still speak more slowly than Oksana and Taras.
lines.source_literal: I-thank! But I still speak more-slowly, than Oksana and Taras.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Вони́ украї́нці! Не тре́ба говори́ти шви́дше. Тре́ба бі́льше говори́ти й чита́ти.
lines.source: They're Ukrainians! You don't need to speak faster. You need to speak and read more.
lines.source_literal: They Ukrainians! Not necessary to-speak faster. Necessary more to-speak and to-read.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А яка́ кни́га для ме́не найкра́ща?
lines.source: And which book is best for me?
lines.source_literal: And which book for me best?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Ось ця. Вона́ ле́гша за ту й ду́же ціка́ва.
lines.source: This one. It's easier than that one, and very interesting.
lines.source_literal: Here this. It easier than that and very interesting.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Дя́кую! Я прочита́ю її́ якнайшви́дше.
lines.source: Thank you! I'll read it as fast as I can.
lines.source_literal: I-thank! I will-read it as-fast-as-possible.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Не тре́ба якнайшви́дше. Чита́йте пові́льно, але́ щодня́.
lines.source: There's no need to hurry. Read slowly, but every day.
lines.source_literal: Not necessary as-fast-as-possible. Read slowly, but every-day.

grammar.title: The comparative: '-іш-' and '-ш-'
grammar.explanation:
English compares adjectives in two ways: with an ending for short words ('newer', 'newest') and with a separate word for long ones ('more interesting', 'most interesting'). Ukrainian uses a suffix for nearly every adjective, short or long. The plain adjective, the comparative and the superlative are called the three degrees of comparison. The comparative says that something has more of a quality than something else: 'нові́ший', newer. The superlative says that it has the most: 'найнові́ший', newest. Note 4 explains the superlative.

To form the comparative, take the stem, which is the adjective without its ending '-ий', add a suffix, and then add the ordinary adjective ending again. There are two suffixes:

- '-іш-' for most adjectives: 'нови́й', 'нові́ший'; 'ціка́вий', 'ціка́віший'; 'холо́дний', 'холодні́ший'; 'те́плий', 'теплі́ший'
- '-ш-' for a smaller group of common adjectives, most of them about size, age, speed, weight or price: 'шви́дкий', 'шви́дший'; 'молоди́й', 'моло́дший'; 'деше́вий', 'деше́вший'

No rule tells you which suffix an adjective takes, so learn the comparative with each adjective of the group in the table. An adjective you meet later takes '-іш-' unless its note says otherwise.

Many adjectives of the '-ш-' group have the suffix '-к-', '-ьк-' or '-ок-' after the root, and it drops before '-ш-': 'шви́дкий', 'шви́дший'; 'коро́ткий', 'коро́тший'; 'легки́й', 'ле́гший'. Where the root then ends in 'с', 'з' or 'ж', that consonant merges with the 'ш' of the suffix:

- 'с' and 'ш' are written 'щ': 'висо́кий', 'ви́щий'
- 'з' and 'ш' are written 'жч': 'низьки́й', 'ни́жчий'
- 'ж' and 'ш' are written 'жч': 'важки́й', 'ва́жчий'

In 'дороги́й' the 'г' and the 'ш' are also written 'жч': 'доро́жчий'. In 'ле́гший' the 'г' stays, and in 'до́вший' it drops; these three are learned as they are. Note 6 explains how all of these are said.

A comparative is an ordinary adjective with the hard endings of 'нови́й', and it agrees with its noun in gender, number and case: 'нові́ший телефо́н', 'нові́ша кни́га', 'нові́ше мі́сто', 'нові́ші ку́ртки'; 'Я хо́чу деше́вшу ку́ртку.' (I want a cheaper jacket.) It stands before its noun or is the predicate, with no word for 'is': 'Цей по́їзд шви́дший.' (This train is faster.)

examples.source: My phone is newer.
This book is more interesting.
I want a cheaper hotel.
This suitcase is heavier.
We are going by the faster train.

grammar.title: Better, worse, bigger, smaller, and older and younger
grammar.explanation:
Four very common adjectives form the comparative on a different stem, as English 'good', 'better' and 'bad', 'worse' do:

- 'вели́кий', big: 'бі́льший', bigger
- 'мали́й', small: 'ме́нший', smaller
- 'до́брий', good: 'кра́щий', better
- 'пога́ний', bad: 'гі́рший', worse

'До́брий' is the adjective you know from the greeting 'до́брий день'; it means good or kind. These four comparatives take the same endings as the others ('бі́льша кварти́ра', 'кра́щі ку́ртки') and form the superlative in the same way, with 'най-': 'найбі́льший', 'найкра́щий'.

'Га́рний' has two meanings, and each has its own comparative. When it means good, as in 'га́рна пого́да', the comparative is 'кра́щий': 'кра́ща пого́да', better weather. When it means beautiful, the comparative is the regular form 'гарні́ший', more beautiful.

'Стари́й' also has two comparatives. 'Ста́рший', older, is used for people and their age; 'старі́ший', older, is used for things: 'старі́ший дім', an older house. The comparatives of age, 'ста́рший' and 'моло́дший', also mean senior and junior. With family words they say who was born earlier or later, with no second person named, as English 'older' and 'younger' do:

- 'мій ста́рший брат', my older brother
- 'моя́ моло́дша сестра́', my younger sister
- 'найста́рший син', the oldest son
- 'наймоло́дша до́нька', the youngest daughter

In a sentence without a noun after it, 'Я ста́рша.' (I am older) simply compares the speaker with someone already mentioned.

examples.source: Our apartment is smaller.
The weather is better today.
She is Taras's older sister.
I have a younger sister.
This house is older.

grammar.title: Than: 'ніж' and 'за'
grammar.explanation:
English names the second thing in a comparison after 'than'. Ukrainian has two ways to do it.

The conjunction 'ніж' means 'than'. A comma stands before it, and the word after it is in the same case as the word it is compared with. Most often that is a subject, so the word after 'ніж' is in the nominative, even when it is a pronoun:

- 'Ки́їв бі́льший, ніж Львів.' (Kyiv is bigger than Lviv.)
- 'Тара́с ви́щий, ніж я.' (Taras is taller than I am.)
- 'Я люблю́ лі́то бі́льше, ніж зи́му.' (I love summer more than winter.)

In the third sentence 'зи́му' is accusative, like 'лі́то', because both are objects of 'люблю́'. 'Ніж' can also introduce a place, a time or a whole clause: 'кра́щий, ніж у Ки́єві' (better than in Kyiv), 'холодні́ше, ніж учо́ра' (colder than yesterday), 'ле́гша, ніж я ду́мав' (easier than I thought).

The preposition 'за', which you know as 'behind' with the instrumental, means 'than' when it follows a comparative and takes the accusative. It takes a single noun or pronoun, with no comma: 'Тара́с ви́щий за ме́не.' (Taras is taller than me.) The accusative of a masculine or neuter thing is the same as its nominative ('за Львів'), so the case shows above all in feminine nouns, in people and in pronouns: 'за ма́му', 'за бра́та', 'за ме́не', 'за те́бе', 'за ньо́го', 'за не́ї'. After a preposition, 'мене́' and 'тебе́' move their stress to the first syllable, as in 'у ме́не'.

Both ways are standard and mean the same. 'За' is short and very common in speech; 'ніж' is the only choice before anything other than a single noun or pronoun.

Three words before a comparative say how big the difference is:

- 'тро́хи', a little: 'тро́хи бі́льший', a little bigger
- 'наба́гато', much: 'наба́гато бі́льший', much bigger
- 'ще', which also means still or yet, here means even: 'ще бі́льший', even bigger

An exact difference is 'на' with the accusative: 'Оле́на ста́рша за Тара́са на три ро́ки.' (Olena is three years older than Taras, literally 'Olena older than Taras on three years'.)

rows: Я люблю́ лі́то бі́льше, ніж зи́му.
I love summer more, than winter
I love summer more than winter.
The language is easier than I thought.
This jacket is a little more expensive.
The coffee here is even better.

examples.source: My sister is younger than me.
This hotel is more expensive than that one.

grammar.title: The superlative: 'най-', 'якнай-', and 'більш' and 'менш'
grammar.explanation:
The superlative says that something has a quality to the highest degree: the biggest, the best. Ukrainian forms it by putting the prefix 'най-' before the comparative, and the stress stays where the comparative has it:

- 'бі́льший', 'найбі́льший', biggest
- 'кра́щий', 'найкра́щий', best
- 'нові́ший', 'найнові́ший', newest
- 'ви́щий', 'найви́щий', highest, tallest

Ukrainian has no word for 'the', so 'найбі́льший' alone means 'the biggest'. The superlative agrees like any adjective: 'найбі́льше мі́сто', 'найкра́ща ка́ва', 'найдо́вші дні'. To say where, or among whom, add 'у' or 'в' with the locative, or 'з' with the genitive plural:

- 'найбі́льше мі́сто в Украї́ні', the biggest city in Ukraine
- 'найви́щий у сім’ї́', the tallest in the family
- 'найкра́щий з усі́х', the best of all
- 'хто з нас', which of us

'Усі́х' is the genitive plural of 'всі', all, with 'у' in place of 'в' after a consonant, by the euphony rule.

The prefix 'якнай-' means 'as ... as possible': 'якнайкра́щий', the best possible; 'якнайшви́дше', as fast as possible. It is used above all with adverbs, which the next note explains, and in requests and promises: 'Зроби́ це якнайшви́дше.' (Do it as fast as you can.)

The words 'більш' and 'менш' are shortened forms of 'бі́льше', more, and 'ме́нше', less, used before an adjective. 'Більш ціка́вий' means the same as 'ціка́віший'. The one-word form is usual in speech, and 'більш' is more common in writing and with long adjectives. 'Менш' is the only way to say 'less' with an adjective: 'менш ціка́вий', less interesting; 'менш дороги́й', less expensive. 'Найбі́льш' and 'найме́нш' before an adjective form superlatives: 'найбі́льш ціка́вий', the most interesting; 'найме́нш ціка́вий', the least interesting. A comparative uses either the suffix or 'більш', never both together.

rows: This is the biggest city in Ukraine.
Taras is the tallest of all.
I will read it as fast as I can.
This is the most interesting museum.

grammar.title: Comparing actions, and saying 'as ... as' and 'the same as'
grammar.explanation:
An adverb describes how an action is done: 'шви́дко', quickly; 'до́бре', well. The comparative of an adverb is the comparative adjective with '-е' in place of '-ий': 'шви́дший', 'шви́дше', faster; 'кра́щий', 'кра́ще', better. The most common ones are:

- 'до́бре', well: 'кра́ще', better
- 'пога́но', badly: 'гі́рше', worse
- 'шви́дко', quickly: 'шви́дше', faster
- 'пові́льно', slowly: 'пові́льніше', more slowly
- 'бага́то', a lot: 'бі́льше', more
- 'ма́ло', little: 'ме́нше', less

The superlative adds 'най-' ('найкра́ще', best; 'найбі́льше', most), and 'якнай-' gives 'as ... as possible' ('якнайшви́дше'). 'Ніж' and 'за' work as they do with adjectives: 'Окса́на гово́рить шви́дше, ніж я.' (Oksana speaks faster than I do.)

The adverb 'кра́ще' is spelled like the neuter of the adjective 'кра́щий', but they are two different words. The adjective agrees with a noun: 'кра́ще мі́сто', a better city. The adverb describes a verb and never changes: 'Вона́ співа́є кра́ще.' (She sings better.)

The predicative words 'те́пло' and 'хо́лодно' compare in the same way, and are still the whole predicate of a sentence without a subject: 'Сього́дні теплі́ше, ніж учо́ра.' (It is warmer today than yesterday.) With an infinitive, 'ле́гко', easy, gives 'ле́гше': 'Чита́ти ле́гше, ніж говори́ти.' (Reading is easier than speaking.)

To say that two things are equal or not equal, Ukrainian uses 'таки́й' or 'так' before the adjective or adverb, and 'як' before the second thing. Here 'як' is a conjunction meaning 'as', and a comma stands before it:

- 'таки́й' agrees with the noun and goes with an adjective: 'Ця ку́ртка не така́ дорога́, як та.' (This jacket is not as expensive as that one.)
- 'так' never changes and goes with an adverb or a predicative word: 'Я не бі́гаю так шви́дко, як ти.' (I don't run as fast as you.)

This 'так' is an adverb meaning 'so' or 'in this way', a different word from the particle 'так', yes. Without 'як', the two words mean 'so' or 'such': 'Таки́й до́вгий день!' (Such a long day!); 'Сього́дні так хо́лодно!' (It is so cold today!)

After 'таки́й', the word 'са́мий' means 'same', and both words agree with the noun: 'таки́й са́мий', 'така́ са́ма', 'таке́ са́ме', 'такі́ са́мі'. It is a different word from 'сам', oneself. 'Таки́й са́мий, як' means 'the same as', and 'так са́мо, як' means 'just as' or 'in the same way as'.

rows: Oksana speaks faster than I do.
Taras reads more than I do.
It is warmer today than yesterday.
Ця ку́ртка не така́ дорога́, як та.
this jacket not such expensive, as that
This jacket is not as expensive as that one.
Я не бі́гаю так шви́дко, як ти.
I not run so fast, as you
I don't run as fast as you.
У ме́не така́ са́ма ку́ртка, як у те́бе.
at me such same jacket, as at you
I have the same jacket as you.
Він співа́є так са́мо, як брат.
he sings so same, as brother
He sings just like his brother.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: ле́гший, ни́жчий, ви́щий and the other new words
grammar.explanation:
Every new word and form in this unit can be read with the rules of the alphabet units and the unit on stress. The points below are the ones the comparatives bring up.

Ukrainian keeps a voiced consonant voiced before most other consonants, but 'г' before 'к' or 'т' is said [x], as in 'ле́гко' [ˈlɛxkɔ]. The same happens before 'ш'. So 'легки́й' is [lɛxˈkɪj], and its comparative 'ле́гший' is [ˈlɛxʃɪj]. The spelling keeps the 'г' of the root in every form. The other voiced consonants of this unit stay voiced: 'низьки́й' [nɪzʲˈkɪj] has a soft, voiced 'зь' before 'к', 'важки́й' [ʋɑʒˈkɪj] a voiced 'ж', and 'шви́дкий' [ˈʃʋɪdkɪj] a voiced 'д'. The conjunction 'ніж' ends in a voiced [ʒ], as the noun 'ніж', knife, does.

When the suffix '-ш-' meets the last consonant of the root, the two merge into one spelling:

- 'с' and 'ш' give 'щ', said [ʃt͡ʃ]: 'висо́кий', 'ви́щий' [ˈʋɪʃt͡ʃɪj]
- 'з' and 'ш' give 'жч', said [ʒt͡ʃ]: 'низьки́й', 'ни́жчий' [ˈnɪʒt͡ʃɪj]
- 'ж' and 'ш' give 'жч': 'важки́й', 'ва́жчий' [ˈʋɑʒt͡ʃɪj]
- 'г' and 'ш' give 'жч' in one word of this unit: 'дороги́й', 'доро́жчий' [dɔˈrɔʒt͡ʃɪj]

'Жч' is said like 'щ' with a voiced first sound: [ʒ] and then [t͡ʃ]. 'Кра́щий' [ˈkrɑʃt͡ʃɪj] has the same 'щ' as 'ви́щий'.

Before 'ш', 'д' and 'т' keep their letter but are said with the tongue where 'ш' is made. In 'шви́дший' and 'шви́дше' the 'д' is said [d͡ʒ], the sound of 'дж', and stays voiced: [ˈʃʋɪd͡ʒʃɪj]. In 'коро́тший' the 'т' is said [t͡ʃ], the sound of 'ч': [kɔˈrɔt͡ʃʃɪj].

The letter 'в' is [w] at the end of a syllable, before a consonant: 'до́вгий' [ˈdɔwɦɪj], 'до́вший' [ˈdɔwʃɪj], 'деше́вший' [dɛˈʃɛwʃɪj], and at the end of 'дощі́в'. Before a vowel it is [ʋ]: 'шви́дкий', 'деше́вий'.

The soft sign in 'бі́льший' [ˈbʲilʲʃɪj] and 'більш' keeps the 'л' soft before 'ш'; 'ме́нший' and 'гі́рший' have a hard 'н' and a hard 'р'. Before the 'і' of '-іш-', 'л' and 'н' are soft: 'теплі́ший' [tɛpˈlʲiʃɪj], 'холодні́ший' [xɔlɔdˈnʲiʃɪj].

The stress moves in several comparatives. Adjectives stressed on the ending that take '-ш-' move it to the stem: 'молоди́й', 'моло́дший'; 'дороги́й', 'доро́жчий'; 'легки́й', 'ле́гший'; 'важки́й', 'ва́жчий'; 'низьки́й', 'ни́жчий'. In every comparative with '-ш-' in this unit the stress falls on the syllable just before the suffix: 'ви́щий', 'коро́тший', 'деше́вший'. In comparatives with '-іш-' it is not predictable: 'нові́ший', 'теплі́ший' and 'холодні́ший' stress the 'і', while 'ціка́віший' keeps the stress of 'ціка́вий'. The prefixes 'най-' and 'якнай-' never move the stress: 'найви́щий', 'якнайшви́дше' [jɑknɑjˈʃʋɪd͡ʒʃɛ], a word of four syllables.

culture.title: Kyiv and Lviv, and comparisons in proverbs
culture.text:
Ukrainians like to compare their two best-known cities. Kyiv, the capital, on the Dnipro river, is the largest city in Ukraine, with about three million people. It is also one of the oldest cities of Eastern Europe: in 1982 it celebrated its fifteen hundredth anniversary. Its Saint Sophia Cathedral and its Monastery of the Caves are on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

Lviv, in the west, is much smaller, with about seven hundred thousand people, and much younger: it was founded in the thirteenth century and named after Lev, the son of King Danylo. Its old center, on the World Heritage List since 1998, has narrow streets, squares and old coffeehouses, and Ukrainians often call Lviv the coffee capital of the country. Lviv gets more rain than Kyiv, and its summers are a little cooler.

The country itself is full of superlatives. Ukraine is the largest country that lies entirely in Europe. Its highest mountain is 'Гове́рла', Hoverla, 2,061 meters high, in the Carpathians, and its longest river is 'Дніпро́', the Dnipro.

Many Ukrainian proverbs are comparisons:

- 'Кра́ще пі́зно, ніж ніко́ли.' means 'Better late than never'; 'пі́зно' is late.
- 'У гостя́х до́бре, а вдо́ма кра́ще.' is literally 'at guests well, and at home better': it is pleasant to be a guest, but home is better. 'Гостя́х' is the locative plural of 'гість', guest.
- 'Кра́ще сини́ця в руці́, ніж жураве́ль у не́бі.' is literally 'better titmouse in hand, than crane in sky', and it means the same as the English 'A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush'. 'Сини́ця' is a titmouse, a small bird; 'жураве́ль' is a crane, a large bird that flies high; 'не́бо' is the sky.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian with the English
Match each adjective with its meaning

exercises.explanation: 'До́вгий' means long, for length or time. Short is 'коро́ткий', and young is 'молоди́й'.

exercises.prompt: Which word is the comparative of 'нови́й'?
exercises.explanation: The comparative adds '-іш-' to the stem: 'нові́ший', newer. 'Найнові́ший' is the superlative, newest, and 'нова́' is the feminine of 'нови́й'.

exercises.prompt: Which word is the comparative of 'висо́кий'?
exercises.explanation: The '-ок-' of 'висо́кий' drops, and 'с' with the suffix '-ш-' is written 'щ': 'ви́щий'. 'Ни́жчий' is the comparative of 'низьки́й', and 'до́вший' of 'до́вгий'.

choices: It will be colder tomorrow than today.
It was warmer yesterday than today.
It will be warmer tomorrow than today.

exercises.prompt: Which comparative is formed on a different stem from its adjective?
exercises.explanation: 'Вели́кий', 'мали́й', 'до́брий' and 'пога́ний' form their comparatives on other stems: 'бі́льший', 'ме́нший', 'кра́щий' and 'гі́рший'. The other two add a suffix to their own stem.
'Нови́й' takes '-іш-': 'нові́ший'. It agrees with 'телефо́н', a masculine noun.

exercises.hint_source: This hotel is more expensive than that one.
exercises.explanation: 'Дороги́й' takes '-ш-', and 'г' with 'ш' is written 'жч': 'доро́жчий'. The stress moves to the stem.
'Мали́й' forms its comparative on another stem: 'ме́нший'. 'За' with the accusative names what Lviv is compared with.

exercises.prompt: Which word completes 'Оле́на ни́жча за ___.', meaning 'Olena is shorter than him'?
exercises.explanation: 'За' after a comparative takes the accusative. The accusative of 'він' is 'його́', and after a preposition it begins with 'н': 'за ньо́го'.

exercises.prompt: Which word completes 'Сем ста́рший, ніж ___.', meaning 'Sam is older than she is'?
exercises.explanation: After 'ніж' the word is in the same case as the word it is compared with. 'Сем' is the subject, in the nominative, so the pronoun is in the nominative: 'вона́'.

exercises.prompt_target: Оле́на ___ за Тара́са на три ро́ки.
exercises.hint_source: Olena is three years older than Taras.
exercises.explanation: For people and their age, the comparative of 'стари́й' is 'ста́рший', here feminine because it agrees with 'Оле́на'. 'На' with the accusative gives the difference.

exercises.hint_source: This is the biggest city in Ukraine.
exercises.explanation: The superlative is 'най-' plus the comparative 'бі́льший'. It agrees with 'мі́сто', a neuter noun: 'найбі́льше'.
'Якнай-' before a comparative means 'as ... as possible'. 'Шви́дше' alone means faster.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'my older brother'?
exercises.explanation: With family words, 'ста́рший' says who was born earlier, with no second person named. 'Стари́й брат' means an old brother, and 'найста́рший брат' is the oldest brother.

exercises.hint_source: Taras runs faster than I do.
exercises.explanation: A verb is compared with an adverb: 'шви́дко' becomes 'шви́дше'.

exercises.prompt_target: У Тара́са таки́й ___ телефо́н, як у ме́не.
exercises.hint_source: Taras has the same phone as I do.
exercises.explanation: 'Таки́й са́мий, як' means 'the same as', and both words agree with the noun, here the masculine noun 'телефо́н'.

exercises.hint_source: It is not as cold today as yesterday.
exercises.explanation: 'Хо́лодно' is a predicative word, so it takes 'так', which never changes. 'Таки́й' goes with an adjective and agrees with a noun.

choices: An adverb that says how she sings
exercises.explanation: 'Кра́ще' here describes the verb 'співа́є' and never changes, so it is the adverb, better. The neuter adjective 'кра́ще' agrees with a neuter noun, as in 'кра́ще мі́сто'.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'висо́кий' become 'ви́щий' in the comparative?
choices: 'Ви́щий' is formed on a different stem, like 'бі́льший'.
The '-ок-' drops, and 'с' with the suffix '-ш-' is written 'щ'.
exercises.explanation: The root is 'вис-'. Its suffix '-ок-' drops before the comparative suffix '-ш-', and 'с' and 'ш' merge into 'щ', said [ʃt͡ʃ].

choices: Every 'г' in a comparative is said [x].
The letter in this word is 'ґ'.
'Г' before 'к', 'т' or 'ш' loses its voice and is said [x].
exercises.explanation: Ukrainian keeps voiced consonants voiced before other consonants, with 'г' as the exception: before 'к', 'т' or 'ш' it is said [x], as in 'ле́гко' and 'легки́й'.

exercises.prompt: Why is it 'Тара́с ви́щий, ніж я', but 'Тара́с ви́щий за ме́не'?
choices: 'Ніж' keeps the case of the word compared, here the nominative, and 'за' takes the accusative.
'Ніж' is used for people and 'за' for things.
'Я' is used in speech and 'ме́не' in writing.
exercises.explanation: After 'ніж' the pronoun is in the same case as 'Тара́с', the nominative. The preposition 'за' takes the accusative, 'ме́не'. Both sentences mean 'Taras is taller than me'.

exercises.prompt: In the first dialogue, why does Sam like Kyiv more than Lviv?
choices: It is warmer, and it rains less.
The coffee there is the best in Ukraine.
It is bigger and more interesting, and his friends are there.
exercises.explanation: Sam says 'Він бі́льший і ціка́віший, і тут мої́ дру́зі.' He says that the best coffee is in Lviv, and then that Andrii's is even better.

exercises.prompt: In the second dialogue, why does Olena say that she knows better?
choices: She cooks borscht better than their mother.
exercises.explanation: Olena says 'я ста́рша, і я зна́ю кра́ще'. Taras is the taller one, and both agree that their mother's borscht is the best.

exercises.prompt: In the third dialogue, how does Iryna Petrivna tell Sam to read the book?
exercises.explanation: Sam promises to read it 'якнайшви́дше', and she answers 'Чита́йте пові́льно, але́ щодня́.'

exercises.prompt_source: My mom is shorter than me.
It is warmer in Odesa than in Kyiv.
This is the best café in Kyiv.
This book is not as interesting as that one.

exercises.explanation: 'Висо́кий' gives 'ви́щий'. After 'за' the name is accusative, 'Оле́ну'; after 'ніж' it stays nominative.
The comparative agrees with 'лі́то', a neuter noun: 'теплі́ше'. 'За' takes the accusative form 'зи́му', and 'ніж' keeps the nominative form 'зима́'.
The superlative 'найкра́щий' agrees with 'кни́га', a feminine noun. 'Це' points, so no word for 'is' is needed.
The comparative of the adverb 'пові́льно' is 'пові́льніше'. 'Говорі́ть' is the imperative for 'ви', and 'говори́' for 'ти'.

exercises.hint_source: My brother is older than me.
This suitcase is heavier than that one.
